payload.text:
The amber light catches Greyhollow Ford gone wrong. The ferry sits chained at its post, and the bell that should have called out across the water hangs dead on its post. Tamsin Vale leads the way up from the bank, Brother Odo and Kestrel behind her, boots loud on planks that should have someone's voice over them by now.

The ferry-house door stands open on nothing. Inside: a length of rope cut clean a yard off the floor, swinging slack. The strongbox pried and gaping. And tracks — small, clawed, pressed into the dust — leading not toward the crossing, but down along the causoway, toward the river's dark bend.

Above, a floorboard creaks.

What does Tamsin do?

payload.body: Tamsin Vale, Brother Odo, and Kestrel arrived at Greyhollow Ford to find the ferry chained and its bell silent. The ferry-house door hung open. Inside: a cut rope swinging from the ceiling, a pried strongbox, and small clawed tracks leading toward the river's dark bend rather than the crossing. A floorboard creaked above.
payload.title: The silent bell at Greyhollow Ford

payload.body: The tracks are fresh and made by something small with claws—not human. Whatever cut the rope and broke into the strongbox may still be in the ferry-house; the creak came from above. Full dark is falling.
payload.title: DM: The intruder

payload.text: I search the ferry-house for whoever cut the bell rope.

payload.text:
Tamsin moves room to room, boots stirring dust already disturbed by smaller feet. No one lurks behind the counter, no one crouches by the cold hearth. It's the strongbox that stops her — not just coin spilled across the floor, but the clapper pin from the bell itself, both taken in one go. That creak overhead comes again, closer this time, and when she tips her head back she finds the loft trapdoor ajar, and a shape pressed against the rafters. A hatchet catches what little light there is. Wenna Marsh, white-knuckled, staring down at the three of them like they might be the thing she's hiding from.

What does Tamsin say to her?
Easy now—we're not the ones who dulled your bell, friend. Lower that hatchet before someone's elbow decides for you.

payload.body: Tamsin searched the ferry-house at Greyhollow Ford and found the bell clapper pin scattered with coin from the strongbox. Wenna Marsh, a white-knuckled figure in the loft, holds a hatchet. She watches the party as though they themselves are what she fears.
payload.title: The Bell-Thief at Greyhollow Ford

payload.text: I tell Wenna we will bring Pell home, and ask her for the safe path.

Wenna doesn't lower the hatchet so much as forget it, her arm sagging with the weight of it as Tamsin's words land. "Pell," she says, like testing whether the name still works in her mouth. She climbs down a rung, then another, counting them under her breath — one, two, three — the old habit steadying shaking hands. "Saw 'em take the clapper and the boy both, down past the bend, into the dark water." Her eyes are wet, fierce. "Ferry's chained, bridge is false. There's a causeway path, safe, if the water don't take you first. But you bring him back. Swear it on the old water."
Swear it after we've won, Tamsin — words are cheap, water's not.

payload.body: At the ferry station, Tamsin Vale swore to bring back Pell, Wenna's son. The promise broke through her rage—she lowered her hatchet and descended the ladder with shaking hands. She revealed that someone took both the ferry's clapper and Pell downstream into the dark water. The ferry itself is chained. Wenna named a safe causeway path across the ford, but warned the rising water is a threat. She made Tamsin swear on the old water to return with her son.

payload.text:
The posts lead on, half-sunk, green with slime, marking a path only someone who'd drowned a few secrets would trust. Reeds close overhead, cutting the amber light to threads. Smoke drifts low across the water — cookfire, somewhere close. A voice carries, sing-song, counting coin with the satisfaction of a miser: "Three, four, big-feet's silver, five..." Then another voice, younger, pitched too loud to be anything but scared, trying for brave: "I'm not afraid of you!" Ahead, through a gap in the stalks, a pole juts from the mud — something pale and curved hangs from its crown, swaying slightly.

What does Tamsin do with the camp so close?
Lookout's up on that pole — someone's crown-perch always is.

payload.body: Tamsin followed the old timber posts into the reeds toward the smoke and voices. The path wound through slime-green stalks, cutting off the amber light. A miser's voice counted coin with satisfaction; a younger, frightened voice answered with forced bravery. A pale curved object hung from a pole ahead, swaying in the reeds.

payload.text:
Tamsin steps into the gap where the reeds thin, voice carrying flat across the mud: "What do you want from us?"

The sing-song stops. Snag straightens atop his crooked post, clapper-strap glinting at his waist, grin all teeth. "Toll, big-feet! Reeds are Snag's, water's Snag's — you pay, or you swim home wet and sorry!" He raps the pole twice, lazy, delighted with himself. Beside the fire, Pell Marsh scrambles up too fast, spear wobbling, red rag fluttering. "Don't listen to him — we're not scared of you!" he shouts, far too loud, far too young to mean it the way he wants to.

Behind Snag, shapes rise from the smoke — a goblin settling a dented pot-helm low over its eyes, another easing back from the lookout's crown-perch, spears lifting from where they'd lain forgotten in the mud.

Snag's grin doesn't move. "Pay," he sings again — and the reeds go very still.

What does Tamsin do?

payload.body: Tamsin Vale confronted the stranger blocking the ferry crossing. He is Snag, a goblin who demands toll payment, claiming ownership of the reeds and water. Pell Marsh, a young ferryman, attempted to stand against him but his bluster rang hollow. Snag has at least three goblin companions emerging from the reed-camp fire, armed with spears. The ferry bell hangs silent at Snag's waist on a clapper-strap—he silenced it.

payload.body:
Attempt 1: invented-mechanics: Narration grants Tamsin a near-miss (fire inches away, hair's width from sleeve) with no fact recording a roll or miss. The goblin's attack outcome must come from game state, not prose invention. | player-agency: Narration describes heat washing over Tamsin's face and fire near her sleeve—sensations and physical states of the player character. Only the world's action (the swing, the flame) should be narrated; Tamsin's experience is hers to declare. | [advisory] doctrine: Ending on 'what do you do?' is a list disguised as open choice. Replace with a concrete moment demanding response: the flame arriving, a choice point revealed, or a consequence unfolding.
Attempt 2: invented-mechanics: Narration states 'the goblin by the fire swings it...toward the gap between Tamsin and the reeds, driving her back.' No fact records an attack roll, hit, or forced movement. The attempt may happen, but the world's response (driving her back) is not in the ledger. | [advisory] doctrine: The final line 'Tamsin, the brand swinging close — what do you do?' hands the player an implicit either-or (react to the brand or act otherwise). Better: describe the immediate moment and stop, letting the player define their response.
Attempt 3: invented-mechanics: Narration shows the goblin by the fire attacking Tamsin, but facts state only that this goblin takes its turn; no roll or outcome is recorded. The swing and spark scatter happen without a hit/miss fact. | [advisory] player-agency: Narration decides Snag's physical state, breath, and emotional condition ('where the sing-song used to be'). Snag is an NPC; only the world narrates his words and feelings. | [advisory] doctrine: Narration covers four simultaneous story beats (goblin swing, Snag's state, lookout positioning, Pell's reaction) in one block. Each deserves its own turn. Trim to the immediate threat. | [advisory] doctrine: Ending on 'what do you do?' is a list-style prompt. Better: stop on the incoming brand or a world detail that demands response without asking.

Odo moves fast, dropping to his knees between Tamsin and the firelight, broad shoulders squaring toward the reeds. His hands find the wound and press down hard, murmuring something low under the smoke and crackle of the brand's dying sparks — and the bleeding slows under his palms. Up on his crooked perch, Snag sags against the post, hand still clamped to his own wound, eyes darting between his huddled goblins and the dark treeline beyond the fire, like a man already counting his way out.

Cross the reeds free, only — only let Snag keep breathing, eh?" His goblins glance at each other, spears wavering, none of them looking at the party at all.

payload.text:
The clapper strikes mud and the fight breaks apart on its own weight. Snag's goblins drift from the fire's edge into the reeds, not fleeing, only watching — spears low, eyes catching the dark beyond the coals. Smoke curls thin where the brand still smolders in the mud, and somewhere past the reeds a heron startles, wings loud against the quiet. Pell alone holds ground near the fire, spear raised too high for a boy his size, red rag shaking, chin set hard against being anyone's rescue. The marsh settles into something that isn't quite peace, just a held breath, waiting to see who moves first.

What does Pell do, spear still raised, with no one left to fight?

payload.text: I keep to the old posts and edge toward the reed camp.

Tamsin's foot never finds purchase; the twitch fades in her calf before it starts, and the posts, the chain, the dark water beyond them all stay exactly where they were, unreached. Odo's offered bell catches the firelight instead, and from the reeds a shape unfolds — Snag, stepping out with the clapper-strap cinched at his waist like a trophy belt. "Pretty bell," he sing-songs, "but a bell wants its tongue, big-feet." He taps the strap. "Clapper's mine already. You want the reeds quiet — you give coin on top, or you give blood."

Pell's spear-tip wavers toward the ground, then stops.

What does Pell do now?

Pell's spear wavered, uncertain whether to fight.
